title: Residential energy consumption dynamics: A SHAP-based interpretation, k-means clustering, and predictive modelling
abstract: A proper understanding of climatic consumption dynamics is critical for demand-side management, grid stability, and climate-sensitive residential energy planning. The non-linear interaction between meteorological conditions has necessitated intelligent predictive models. However, existing studies focused on machine learning (ML) models in their black-box nature, with limited interpretability of the impact of climatic-drivers, climatic-demand interactions, and hidden consumption regimes. This research fills this gap through an integrated framework that combines seasonal hypothesis-testing, k-means clustering, Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based interpretability, and advanced predictive modeling using XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), long-short term memory (LSTM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Autoregressive Integrated moving average (ARIMA). The seasonal hypothesis-testing using ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD revealed statistically significant differences in energy consumption across seasons, with peak-demand during winter and summer extremes. SHAP-based feature ranking identified temperature and humidity as the most influential drivers of electricity-demand. The k-means clustering revealed three distinct groups/clusters, which reflect the climatic-consumption scenarios. The ensemble learning (RF and XGBoost) exhibited the lowest training-error. RF had the best training performance with MSE, RMSE, and MAE values of 1.6484, 1.2839, and 0.8480. The data-driven insights in this study provide useful intelligence that supports critical decision-making through a proper understanding of the residential climatic-consumption dynamics. • ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD revealed a significant difference in consumption across seasons • k-means clustering reveals 3 distinct climatic-consumption patterns and regimes • SHAP revealed temperature as a dominant consumption driver • The random forest gave the best training performance with RMSE = 1.2839 • The framework facilitates climate-sensitive demand-side management and planning.

title: Synergistic hybrid systems of 2D-MOFs and TMDs for advanced energy harvesting
abstract: The globally trending move towards renewable energy sources requires materials capable of harvesting, storing, and converting energy in a competent fashion and yet scalable, robust, and affordable. Two-dimensional metal-organic frameworks (2D-MOFs) and transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have been promising materials for photovoltaics, thermoelectrics, piezoelectrics, and triboelectrics, respectively, but both material families are plagued by intrinsic drawbacks. MOFs have high area and chemical tailoring but are hampered by low conductivity, and TMDs have robust electronic and catalytic functionality but are plagued by stability and scalability issues. Recent developments indicate hybrid 2D-MOF/TMD systems are capable of offsetting failings by encapsulating complementary properties, facilitating superior charge separation, band alignment engineering, and enhancement in environmental tolerance. This review critically examines the structural, electronic, and functional synergies of 2D-MOF/TMD hybrids with emphasis on synthesis strategies, interface engineering, defect modulation, and emerging applications in diverse energy harvesting platforms. Comparative analyses of existing studies highlight how hybrid architectures deliver higher power densities, longer cycling stability, and superior device integration relative to their parent materials. Critical issues such as scalable synthesis, long-term stability under operating conditions, and reproducible device-level integration are also mentioned as hurdles in commercialization. Experimental design, computational modeling, and machine learning are envisaged in the future to accelerate discovery and optimization of high-performance hybrids. Bridging the gap between applied engineering and basic research, 2D-MOF/TMD hybrids are a paradigm shift in multifunctional materials and a promising avenue towards next-generation sustainable energy technology.

title: Battery thermal management of electric vehicles: A review and bibliometric analysis of liquid cooling methods
abstract: Thermal management plays a vital role in the operation of electric vehicle (EV) batteries, directly influencing their efficiency, safety, and market adoption. In real-world EV operation, inadequate thermal regulation can accelerate battery degradation and increase safety risks, highlighting the importance of effective battery thermal management system (BTMS) design. In response, extensive research explored liquid BTMSs for EV applications. Despite this growing body of research, a comprehensive overview that combines a critical review and a bibliometric analysis of EV liquid BTMS research remains scarce. This paper aims to address this gap by presenting a combined critical review and bibliometric investigation of recent trends and developments in EV liquid BTMSs. The review examines key aspects of liquid BTMSs, including system configurations, coolant types, performance enhancement methods, and hybrid configurations. The bibliometric analysis covers research and review publications included in the Scopus database from 2015 to 2025, extracted on the 29 th of October 2025. The technical review was updated separately to include selected 2026 publications. After screening, 472 publications strongly related to liquid BTMSs were identified. The analysis demonstrates continuous growth in the field with an annual growth rate of 40.97% and a low average document age of 3.19 years. China leads the research with 214 publications. Liquid BTMS keyword analysis highlights three main research themes: temperature control and coolant systems, EV applications and battery technologies, and battery modeling and simulation. Key research gaps include coupled electrothermal modeling and artificial intelligence-based predictive control. This review highlights recent advancements and research gaps that can guide future development of liquid BTMS design and optimization to improve EV performance and safety.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework for Performance Prediction and Parameter Identification of Microbial Fuel Cells
abstract: Bioelectrochemical systems (BES) such as microbial fuel cells (MFCs) offer a promising route for sustainable wastewater treatment and bioelectricity generation. However, MFC modeling faces a structural dichotomy: mechanistic models provide physical interpretability but suffer from difficult calibration, while data-driven approaches offer predictive flexibility at the cost of mechanistic transparency and limited extrapolation. To reconcile these paradigms, we developed BioElec-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that couples sparse experimental data with a differential-algebraic bioelectrochemical model that distinguishes bulk and biofilm substrate compartments through a mass-transfer coefficient. This paper presents the BioElec-PINN architecture and evaluates its performance on fed-batch MFCs treating synthetic winery wastewater across varying organic loads. We trained the network to jointly reconstruct model-conditioned latent states and estimate ten regularized cycle-specific kinetic, transport, and electrochemical parameters. The BioElec-PINN achieved calibration voltage normalized root mean square error NRMSE values of 0.048–0.100. The inferred parameter sets were subsequently transferred without recalibration to a Radau IIA solver (classical solver), whose forward trajectories showed close cycle-level agreement and supported the cross-formulation dynamic consistency of the learned mechanistic parameterization. A matched Direct multilayer perceptron MLP was additionally evaluated using an interleaved held-out protocol in which approximately 40% of the observations were retained for training and the remaining 60% were used exclusively for raw-data evaluation. The Direct MLP achieved lower pointwise interpolation errors, with mean voltage and chemical oxygen demand (COD) NRMSE values of 0.064 and 0.146, compared with 0.121 and 0.206 for the BioElec-PINN, respectively. A conditional residual-bootstrap analysis based on 20 complete BioElec-PINN retrainings was used to quantify parameter uncertainty. Thirty-three of the forty cycle-specific estimates exhibited relative 95% interval widths below 1%, while the bootstrap correlation structure revealed coordinated kinetic, mediator, and electrochemical parameter groups. However, the unconstrained MLP introduced non-monotonic COD trajectories in three cycles and physically inadmissible continuation outside the observed interval, including negative voltage and substantial COD rebound. In contrast, the BioElec-PINN preserved monotonic substrate depletion and coupled voltage–substrate dynamics while reconstructing model-conditioned latent states and estimating regularized cycle-specific effective parameters. The framework therefore provides a physically structured inverse-calibration component for future MFC digital twins, with raw-data performance, physical admissibility, parameter transferability, and conditional uncertainty evaluated explicitly.
